skill.title: Select a simple random sample and spot bias

candidates.question:
A teacher numbers her 300 students from 1 to 300 and uses a random number generator to pick 25 different numbers. Every student is equally likely to be chosen.
Find the probability that a particular student is in the sample.

steps.title: Say why the method is a simple random sample

lines.text: Every student has the same chance of selection, so there is no bias.

steps.title: (i) Pick the classes that could be over 100

lines.text: The class 90 to 120 includes students above 100, and every class above it is entirely above 100.
At most, all 59 students in 90 to 120 read for more than 100 minutes.

steps.title: (iii) Say why the sampling method is limited

lines.text: Only the first 200 students to arrive were asked, so the sample is not random.
These could be local students, or students arriving together on school buses.
Students who arrive later are left out, so the sample may not be representative.

skill.title: Relate confidence level, sample size and interval width
skill.output: wider/narrower; n needed for a margin

lines.text: A higher confidence level needs a larger $z$-value, so the margin of error, and the interval, gets wider.
$\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})$ increases as $\hat{p}$ rises towards $0.5$ and then decreases, so the standard error does not always increase.
With $n$ fixed, the standard error is the square root of $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})$ divided by $n$, so it rises whenever $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})$ rises.
Increasing $n$ makes $\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}$ smaller, so the standard error always decreases.

steps.title: Set up the margin of error equation

candidates.question:
A 95% confidence interval for a population proportion is constructed from a random sample of size $n = 200$. The margin of error is $0.06$.
The sample proportion $\hat{p}$ stays the same. Find the sample size needed to reduce the margin of error to $0.03$, at the same confidence level.

steps.title: Write the margin of error using n

lines.text: Let $k = 1.96\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}$. It does not change, so the margin of error is $\frac{k}{\sqrt{n}}$.

steps.title: Divide the second by the first

lines.text: Halving the margin of error needs 4 times the sample size.

skill.title: Interpret an analysis and relate it to the original question

candidates.question:
A survey asks 400 randomly chosen people whether they prefer brand A to brand B. 56% prefer brand A. The margin of error is $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$, where $n$ is the sample size.
Find the lower end of the interval for the true percentage who prefer A, and use it to say whether most people prefer A.

lines.text: The true percentage is likely to be between $51\%$ and $61\%$.
The whole interval is above $50\%$, so the survey suggests that most people prefer brand A.

candidates.question:
A games company claims that 40% of its players buy an upgrade. A random sample of players gives a 95% confidence interval of $[43.1\%,\ 52.9\%]$ for the true percentage who buy an upgrade.
Find the sample percentage, which is the centre of the interval, and say whether the interval supports the company's claim.

steps.title: Compare the claim with the interval

lines.text: The claimed $40\%$ is outside the interval, so reject $H_0$.
The sample does not support the claim. The percentage of players who buy an upgrade is probably higher than $40\%$.

candidates.question:
A school says the mean time its students spend on homework is 50 minutes. A random sample of 100 students has a mean of 52 minutes and a standard deviation of 10 minutes. Test $H_0: \mu = 50$ against $H_1: \mu \ne 50$ at the 5% level of significance.
Find the test statistic $z$ and use it to state your conclusion.

lines.text: Use $z = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu}{s / \sqrt{n}}$.
At the 5% level, two-tailed, the critical values are $\pm 1.96$.
$z$ is outside $[-1.96,\ 1.96]$, so reject $H_0$. There is evidence that the mean homework time is not $50$ minutes. It is probably longer.

candidates.question:
In a poll of 400 randomly chosen voters, $46\%$ said they would vote for Ciara in an election between two candidates.
Use the margin of error $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ to find an interval for the true percentage of voters who support Ciara, and say whether the poll shows she will win.

lines.text: The true percentage is likely to be between $41\%$ and $51\%$.
The interval includes values below $50\%$ and above $50\%$, so the poll does not show that Ciara will win. The result is too close to call.
